deciding_marker_or_seam: The siege and vessel transfer move into the king's selection order, ration, named Judean youths, and completed renaming at 1:7; Daniel's new resolve begins at 1:8.
boundary_rationale: I retain 1:1-7 because the royal intake and identity reassignment form the tale's full setup, and the adversative resolve at 1:8 supplies a stronger action seam than the earlier administrative details.
rejected_alternative: Extending the opening through 1:8 would absorb the first act of resistance into exposition, while ending at 1:5 would strand the named youths and their imposed court names.
defensible_basis: The passage establishes place, coercive court program, food provision, participants, and changed names before any participant initiates the test. Those exposition functions reach a natural close at the four completed renamings.

source_observations.text: In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it.
The prince of the eunuchs gave names to them: to Daniel he gave the name Belteshazzar; to Hananiah, Shadrach; to Mishael, Meshach; and to Azariah, Abednego.

primary_reviews.support: The participant list and sequence of imposed names conclude before the volitional turn at 1:8; no textual marker is being made authoritative.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The ration introduced at 1:5 anticipates the food test and gives the exposition a forward dependency.

primary_reviews.support: Selection, training, ration, naming, and identity pressure cohere as the situation that the next scene answers.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The larger chapter-one formation story remains necessary to understand why this setup matters.

primary_reviews.support: A setup child is retrievable if siege, vessels, court service, food, and names continue to hydrate through the complete chapter parent.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Detached retrieval could invite ungoverned chronology or deportation harmonization across Kings, Chronicles, and Jeremiah.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Daniel's resolve opens the request at 1:8, negotiation produces a ten-day test, and the steward's replacement of the assigned provisions records the result at 1:16.
boundary_rationale: The test closes when its observable result changes the steward's practice, so I expose 1:8-16 while requiring the chapter parent to prevent the food episode from being detached from later enablement and examination.
rejected_alternative: Keeping 1:8-21 whole would blur the completed request-test-outcome chain with the new divine enablement and royal examination movement introduced at 1:17.
defensible_basis: Resolve, request, risk objection, proposed trial, consent, comparison, and changed diet form a complete experimental scene. The scene has its own initiating decision and a narrated administrative consequence.

source_observations.text: But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s delicacies, nor with the wine which he drank. Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.
So the steward took away their delicacies and the wine that they were given to drink, and gave them vegetables.

primary_reviews.support: The test's request and ten-day comparison are internally complete through the steward action at 1:16.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: No MT section mark follows 1:16, and the test remains joined to all four youths' court success.

challenges.claim: The child could overstate a seam unsupported by a formal section marker.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Retain mandatory hydration with 1:1-21 and its 1:17-21 sibling.

primary_reviews.support: A resolve, negotiated trial, measured outcome, and steward response give this food-test scene a complete dramatic arc.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The benefits later confirmed before the king cannot be treated as unrelated to the test.

primary_reviews.support: The span is sufficiently intelligible when its exposition and subsequent examination are attached as mandatory context.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Isolating the food choice could turn a narrated court test into a universal dietary rule.

deciding_marker_or_seam: The subject resets to all four youths at 1:17, divine gifts replace the diet trial as the focus, and the appointed examination leads to standing and the Cyrus tenure notice.
boundary_rationale: I begin at 1:17 because its subject reset and gift statement launch the royal-examination movement, which then closes the chapter with service and tenure rather than extending the earlier diet negotiation.
rejected_alternative: Absorbing these verses into 1:8-16 would treat enablement, examination, and long-range tenure as though they were merely the final measurement of the ten-day food test.
defensible_basis: The four youths become the grammatical and narrative center, the king evaluates them at the end of the appointed training period, and 1:21 supplies a temporal coda beyond the immediate test scene.

source_observations.text: Now as for these four youths, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom; and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.
Daniel continued even to the first year of King Cyrus.

primary_reviews.support: The four-youth subject and gift vocabulary at 1:17 differ from the request and comparison language before it.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The absence of a section marker and the chapter's continuous formation plot argue against independent presentation.

challenges.claim: The new child could look like an unrelated prosperity coda.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Pair it bidirectionally with 1:8-16 inside 1:1-21.

primary_reviews.support: Enablement, end-of-training audience, superior examination, court standing, and tenure belong to one success-and-service close.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The royal examination completes the pressure and testing established earlier in the tale.

primary_reviews.support: Retrieval can surface the examination coda so long as names, food pressure, and the preceding test accompany it.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The Cyrus notice is chronology-bearing and could prompt historical harmonization beyond this boundary task.

deciding_marker_or_seam: The troubled dream opens the royal demand, repeated exchanges escalate impossibility and threat, and the issued death decree reaches Daniel and his companions at 2:13.
boundary_rationale: The crisis dialogue should remain intact through the decree's execution stage because 2:13 completes the peril generated by the king's demand; Daniel's answer begins a distinct rescue initiative next.
rejected_alternative: Splitting individual royal and Chaldean speeches would atomize one intensifying negotiation, while continuing into 2:14 would cross into Daniel's prudent intervention.
defensible_basis: Every speech turn advances the same unresolved demand until the court's failure becomes a lethal decree. The search for Daniel at the close creates the handoff to a new responder and strategy.

source_observations.text: In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar dreamed dreams; and his spirit was troubled, and his sleep went from him.
So the decree went out, and the wise men were to be slain. They sought Daniel and his companions to be slain.

primary_reviews.support: Repeated court dialogue remains one Aramaic crisis sequence whose consequence is the decree and search at 2:12-13.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The mid-verse language transition at 2:4b is major book-form evidence but cannot be represented as a verse-level boundary.

primary_reviews.support: Dream disturbance, impossible demand, failed negotiation, and death order make one escalating court scene.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Several speech turns are individually memorable and could tempt conversational atomization.

primary_reviews.support: Keeping the demand with its decree prevents the claim of impossibility from being severed from the king's coercive response.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The whole Daniel 2 parent is still needed before drawing kingdom or wisdom relations elsewhere in Scripture.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Daniel answers Arioch with counsel, learns why the decree is urgent, and obtains time from the king; movement to his house and companions starts only at 2:17.
boundary_rationale: I separate 2:14-16 as the concise intervention that converts imminent execution into time for response; its brevity is offset by mandatory sibling and chapter hydration, not by merging unlike forms.
rejected_alternative: Retaining 2:14-23 as one block would erase the court-to-house location change and fuse the successful intervention with the communal petition, revelation, and hymn it enables.
defensible_basis: The scene has a distinct interlocutor, place, immediate objective, and achieved result: the execution officer explains the crisis and Daniel secures time. A marked transition follows before prayer begins.

source_observations.text: Then Daniel returned answer with counsel and prudence to Arioch the captain of the king’s guard, who had gone out to kill the wise men of Babylon.
Daniel went in, and desired of the king that he would appoint him a time, and he would show the king the interpretation.

primary_reviews.support: A pe after 2:16 corroborates the completed court intervention before Daniel goes home.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The gained time has no independent purpose apart from the petition and revelation that immediately follow.

challenges.claim: A three-verse scene risks becoming a procedural fragment.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Require the 2:17-23 sibling and full dream-crisis parent in retrieval.

primary_reviews.support: Arioch dialogue and the time request complete one intervention before location and participant changes.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The scene's success is proved only by the household response and later court appearance.

primary_reviews.support: Hydrated retrieval preserves prudence, communal dependence, and revelation as sequential parts of one rescue.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Unpaired display might overemphasize court technique while suppressing the prayer movement.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Daniel enters his house, informs his companions, seeks mercy, receives the secret in a night vision, and answers with a completed hymn of praise through 2:23.
boundary_rationale: The house scene deserves its own child because petition, revelation, and hymn complete an interior response before Daniel returns to the execution crisis; the preceding intervention remains required context.
rejected_alternative: Merging backward into 2:14-16 would obscure the new location and communal prayer, while extending to 2:24 would cross from thanksgiving into renewed action before Arioch.
defensible_basis: Household assembly, petition, disclosed secret, and poetic response form a prayer-answer-praise movement. The therefore at 2:24 converts received revelation into the next courtward action.

source_observations.text: Then Daniel went to his house and made the thing known to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, his companions:
I thank you and praise you, O God of my fathers, who have given me wisdom and might, and have now made known to me what we desired of you; for you have made known to us the king’s matter.”

primary_reviews.support: The pe-supported house transition and hymn closure distinguish this response from court negotiation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The petition is causally inseparable from the time request and death decree.

challenges.claim: The hymn could be detached as abstract wisdom praise.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Keep petition, revelation, and praise together under Daniel 2.

primary_reviews.support: Companions, request for mercy, night disclosure, and Daniel's answer trace one complete communal response.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The movement resolves only an intermediate crisis; the dream still must be presented to the king.

primary_reviews.support: The prayer and hymn can be recovered without isolating a divine attribute list from the peril and answer that occasion it.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later canonical echoes must not turn the hymn into automatic graph or theological authority.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Daniel returns to Arioch, enters before the king, attributes disclosure, reports the image and stone, announces the interpretation at 2:36, and closes with the certainty formula at 2:45.
boundary_rationale: I keep 2:24-45 whole because the narrated dream is the evidence interpreted by the second half, and the certainty declaration closes their commissioned presentation before royal recognition begins.
rejected_alternative: Separating dream report from interpretation at 2:36 would make either half incomplete, and isolating 2:44 would detach its kingdom claim from image, metals, stone, and concluding warrant.
defensible_basis: The king's impossible demand requires both recovered dream and interpretation. Framing dialogue, report, explanation, and assurance jointly answer that demand before the king responds in 2:46.

source_observations.text: Therefore Daniel went in to Arioch, whom the king had appointed to destroy the wise men of Babylon. He went and said this to him: “Don’t destroy the wise men of Babylon. Bring me in before the king, and I will show to the king the interpretation.”

Because you saw that a stone was cut out of the mountain without hands, and that it broke in pieces the iron, the bronze, the clay, the silver, and the gold, the great God has made known to the king what will happen hereafter. The dream is certain, and its interpretation sure.”

primary_reviews.support: The report-interpretation formula at 2:36 articulates two phases inside one answer, not two self-sufficient objects.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Section marks and the formula permit internal navigation to report and explanation.

primary_reviews.support: Court entry, recovered image sequence, interpretation, and certainty statement fulfill one narrative commission.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The length and symbolic density could motivate subordinate indexing, but not top-level severance.

primary_reviews.support: The complete span supplies the immediate interpretive frame needed for every famous kingdom or stone clause.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Direct queries to 2:44 are likely and can bypass even this child unless hydration is enforced.

challenges.claim: Verse-level retrieval may still proof-text the enduring kingdom statement.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Always attach 2:24-45 and the complete Daniel 2 macro parent to 2:44.

deciding_marker_or_seam: The king's bodily response, confession about revealed secrets, gifts, promotion, and Daniel's appointment of his companions all follow the completed interpretation and close the death-decree reversal.
boundary_rationale: The royal response stands as a compact closure because it changes from disclosure to recognition and appointment, yet it remains parent-bound to the crisis whose threatened deaths these promotions reverse.
rejected_alternative: Including this response in 2:24-45 would combine the commissioned dream interpretation with its court consequence; separating individual promotions would fracture one reversal coda.
defensible_basis: A new actor responds after the certainty formula, and every remaining verse concerns recognition or changed status. Daniel's request for his companions completes the rescue begun when all wise men faced death.

source_observations.text: Then King Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face, worshiped Daniel, and commanded that they should offer an offering and sweet odors to him.
Daniel requested of the king, and he appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the affairs of the province of Babylon, but Daniel was in the king’s gate.

primary_reviews.support: The king's response begins after the interpretation closure and maintains one recognition-promotion register.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its claims presuppose the preceding revelation and cannot function as independent source-language testimony.

primary_reviews.support: Recognition, gifts, office, and companion appointments provide the court tale's coherent reversal ending.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The coda is short and entirely caused by Daniel's preceding performance.

primary_reviews.support: Attaching the parent keeps royal confession and promotion inside the impossible-demand narrative rather than abstracting them.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The king's language must not become an unqualified doctrinal formulation outside the story.

deciding_marker_or_seam: The image is erected, officials assemble, the herald gives the music-triggered command and furnace penalty, and the gathered peoples enact compliance at 3:7 before an accusation begins.
boundary_rationale: I retain the whole dedication sequence because its repeated officials, instruments, peoples, and image language builds one public command-and-compliance scene whose contrast arrives with the accusers.
rejected_alternative: Breaking apart the official or instrument lists would destroy their cumulative ceremonial function, while continuing through 3:8 would cross from public compliance to targeted accusation.
defensible_basis: Construction, convocation, herald speech, sanction, and mass response comprise the full coercive spectacle. Repetition performs the decree in narrative time rather than supplying separable catalog entries.

source_observations.text: Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was sixty cubits and its width six cubits. He set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.

Therefore at that time, when all the peoples heard the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipe, and all kinds of music, all the peoples, the nations, and the languages fell down and worshiped the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up.

primary_reviews.support: Repeated Aramaic lists bind convocation, command, and compliance rather than signaling separate lexical units.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The lists contain internal formulae that can support navigation without authorizing new chunks.

primary_reviews.support: The spectacle reaches completion only when the summoned population responds to the herald's threatened command.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The furnace penalty points forward to the peril scene and keeps the whole tale as parent.

primary_reviews.support: One exposure-compliance span keeps image worship and coercion contextualized before the dissenting answer.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Canonical links to image prohibitions are evidence only and must not imply direct dependence.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Accusers report noncompliance, the king summons the three men and repeats the ultimatum, and their complete two-part answer ends at 3:18 before his appearance changes in fury.
boundary_rationale: The accusation and hearing remain together because the accusers' claim is tested in the king's direct ultimatum and the defendants' response; fury at 3:19 initiates the ordeal rather than continuing debate.
rejected_alternative: A cut after the accusation at 3:12 would detach charge from hearing, while isolating 3:17-18 would remove the royal threat and the full answer's immediate cause.
defensible_basis: Charge, confrontation, renewed threat, question about deliverance, and refusal form a courtroom exchange. The shift to furnace action at 3:19 closes speech and opens execution of the penalty.

source_observations.text: Therefore at that time certain Chaldeans came near and brought accusation against the Jews.
But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image which you have set up.”

primary_reviews.support: Accusation formula, royal interrogation, and the three men's answer are adjacent speech actions in one hearing.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A section mark after 3:12 distinguishes accusation from confrontation but does not make either sufficient alone.

primary_reviews.support: The repeated decree becomes personal ultimatum and receives a complete refusal before the narrative changes to punishment.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The answer anticipates the ordeal and must remain linked to what follows as well as what precedes.

primary_reviews.support: The span protects the balance between ability to deliver and refusal even if deliverance does not occur.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Queries often isolate 3:17-18 and could turn a situational answer into a generalized rescue guarantee.

challenges.claim: The famous refusal can still surface without the ultimatum or furnace outcome.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Enforce both 3:8-18 and the complete chapter-three parent during retrieval.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Fury initiates heating, binding, and casting; the king then sees four walking figures, summons the three, and assembled officials verify their unharmed bodies at 3:27.
boundary_rationale: I end the ordeal after official inspection because the threatened penalty has then been enacted and publicly reversed; Nebuchadnezzar's blessing at 3:28 changes the mode from witnessed event to interpretive decree.
rejected_alternative: Retaining 3:19-30 would combine ordeal and verification with the new royal blessing-decree form at 3:28, whereas stopping at 3:23 would leave deliverance unreported.
defensible_basis: Execution of the sentence, lethal furnace heat, royal astonishment, release, and multisensory inspection trace one peril-to-verification sequence. The public finding supplies the premise for the proclamation that follows.

source_observations.text: Then Nebuchadnezzar was full of fury, and the form of his appearance was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He spoke, and commanded that they should heat the furnace seven times more than it was usually heated.

The local governors, the deputies, and the governors, and the king’s counselors, being gathered together, saw these men, that the fire had no power on their bodies. The hair of their head wasn’t singed. Their pants weren’t changed. The smell of fire wasn’t even on them.

primary_reviews.support: Execution verbs, royal sight report, summons, and official inspection carry the ordeal through its observable result.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Internal marks after 3:23 and 3:25 articulate stages without supplying stronger top-level closures.

primary_reviews.support: The verification at 3:27 completes the furnace action before proclamation begins.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The decree interprets the rescue and belongs to the tale's reversal rather than functioning independently.

challenges.claim: The coda split may hide the decree's causal dependence on deliverance.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Bind 3:19-27 and 3:28-30 under the complete image-and-furnace parent.

primary_reviews.support: Keeping inspection with the ordeal prevents the fourth figure or unharmed bodies from surfacing as contextless atoms.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: No identity for the fourth figure, miracle mechanism, or typological equation is settled.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Nebuchadnezzar begins a blessing at 3:28, converts it into a universal punitive decree at 3:29, and closes with promotion in 3:30.
boundary_rationale: The proclamation coda remains one unit so blessing, coercive penalty, and promotion stay visible together rather than allowing a praise statement to be retrieved apart from its violent and political aftermath.
rejected_alternative: Merging this coda with 3:19-27 would conceal the shift from narrated verification to royal proclamation, while separating blessing, threat, and promotion would sanitize their combined closure.
defensible_basis: The same royal speaker interprets the witnessed rescue, legislates a violent sanction, and changes the three men's status. These linked speech-and-action consequences close the public court tale.

source_observations.text: Nebuchadnezzar spoke and said, “Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent his angel and delivered his servants who trusted in him, and have changed the king’s word, and have yielded their bodies, that they might not serve nor worship any god except their own God.
Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the province of Babylon.

primary_reviews.support: A single royal response sequence joins blessing, decree formula, penalty, and promotion.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The coda has no narrative basis without the verified deliverance immediately before it.

primary_reviews.support: The transition to formal proclamation is clear enough to identify a child movement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Decree and promotion complete the reversal generated by the furnace event.

challenges.claim: A separate coda might be mistaken for a self-standing royal confession.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Hydrate the accusation, refusal, ordeal, and public inspection whenever this child surfaces.

primary_reviews.support: The chosen limits retain the praise, punitive decree, and office change in one ethically complete aftermath.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later use of the blessing must not omit the threatened dismemberment and tale context.

deciding_marker_or_seam: The king addresses all peoples, announces his purpose to recount signs, and states a hymnic kingdom thesis before first-person palace rest and dream disturbance begin at 4:4.
boundary_rationale: I preserve the three-verse prologue because it names the audience, purpose, and thesis that the subsequent dream-fulfillment story demonstrates; the palace scene at 4:4 is a genuine narrative reset.
rejected_alternative: Joining the address directly to the dream report would blur the proclamation frame, while isolating 4:3 would remove the declared purpose and audience that give the praise its rhetorical function.
defensible_basis: Epistolary-style address, programmatic announcement, and opening praise establish the form and interpretive horizon of the entire chapter-four proclamation. A new narrative situation follows them.

source_observations.text: Nebuchadnezzar the king, to all the peoples, nations, and languages, who dwell in all the earth: Peace be multiplied to you.
How great are his signs! How mighty are his wonders! His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom. His dominion is from generation to generation.

primary_reviews.support: Address, purpose formula, and praise constitute an Aramaic proclamation opening before the narrated dream.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: These lines frame the whole chapter and should not be treated as a detachable doctrinal statement.

primary_reviews.support: The prologue announces exactly the signs-and-wonders story that follows and closes before the palace recollection.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its thesis finds narrative proof only through dream, abasement, restoration, and closing praise.

primary_reviews.support: A framed opening can be indexed while still forcing retrieval of the complete royal testimony.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Universal address and kingdom language may otherwise be generalized beyond their proclamation setting.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Rest in the palace gives way to fear, failed interpreters, Daniel's arrival, the tree vision, watcher decree, stated purpose, and the king's renewed request at 4:18.
boundary_rationale: The dream stays whole from palace setting through the final request because tree and decree are mutually defining parts of what Daniel must interpret; his astonishment at 4:19 begins the answer scene.
rejected_alternative: Splitting at Daniel's arrival or the watcher speech would divide one dream as narrated by the king, and extending into 4:19 would cross into Daniel's emotional pause and interpretation.
defensible_basis: Narrative frame, symbolic tree, descending watcher, decree, and explicit request for interpretation form a complete dream report. The king remains the first-person reporter throughout the embedded vision.

source_observations.text: I, Nebuchadnezzar, was at rest in my house, and flourishing in my palace.

“This dream I, King Nebuchadnezzar, have seen; and you, Belteshazzar, declare the interpretation, because all the wise men of my kingdom are not able to make known to me the interpretation; but you are able, for the spirit of the holy gods is in you.”

primary_reviews.support: First-person narration and the embedded watcher command remain inside one presented dream through the interpretation request.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Daniel's arrival and direct address create internal speech transitions suitable for annotation.

primary_reviews.support: Palace setting, fearful image, symbolic sequence, decree, and appeal to the interpreter produce a complete vision-report form.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The dream remains unresolved until the interpretation and fulfillment movements later in the proclamation.

primary_reviews.support: Tree and watcher material stays joined before any canonical comparison to prophetic tree imagery.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: No identity, diagnosis, historical equation, or independent relation is authorized by the imagery.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Daniel's alarm opens the answer, tree and watcher details are applied in sequence, the restoration condition is explained, and direct counsel concludes the interpretation at 4:27.
boundary_rationale: I close at the counsel because Daniel has completed both exposition and response to the dream; the concise fulfillment hinge that follows is kept out of this accepted unit while its attachment remains separately held.
rejected_alternative: Attaching the fulfillment formula at 4:28 backward is a viable alternative, but the active route leaves it with realization so the counsel remains the final speech act of this interpretive exchange.
defensible_basis: Interpreter reaction, reassurance, symbolic identification within the local discourse, consequence, duration, restoration, and ethical counsel proceed as one uninterrupted answer to the reported dream.

source_observations.text: Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was stricken mute for a while, and his thoughts troubled him. The king answered, “Belteshazzar, don’t let the dream or the interpretation, trouble you.” Belteshazzar answered, “My lord, may the dream be for those who hate you, and its interpretation to your adversaries.

Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to you, and break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor. Perhaps there may be a lengthening of your tranquility.”

primary_reviews.support: Daniel's emotional onset and continuous answer culminate in second-person counsel before the fulfillment formula.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The pe-closed formula at WEB 4:28 is anaphoric to this interpretation and may hydrate backward.

primary_reviews.support: Interpretation and admonition are one response to the king rather than separate exposition and application chunks.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The counsel points forward to the realization and cannot terminate the chapter's larger argument.

primary_reviews.support: Keeping the counsel with the entire interpretation constrains ethical use by the dream and its narrated outcome.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Canonical pride or tree relations remain context aids, not grounds for enlarging or shrinking the child.

deciding_marker_or_seam: WEB 4:28 states that all came upon the king and is followed by a pe in the MT-family coordinate; twelve months later the boast, heavenly sentence, and abasement unfold through 4:33.
boundary_rationale: I use 4:28-33 as the non-fragmenting active route, but I hold its initial hinge because the pe closes the formula while its semantics simultaneously look backward to interpretation and forward to realization.
rejected_alternative: The strongest rival attaches WEB 4:28 backward to 4:19-27 and starts realization at 4:29; exposing 4:28 alone is rejected because the formula points in both directions.
defensible_basis: Forward attachment avoids a one-verse fragment and lets the fulfillment summary introduce the concrete realization it announces. Yet the formula also closes the interpretation's prediction, so local correlated evidence cannot settle exclusive ownership.

source_observations.text: All this came on the King Nebuchadnezzar.

This was fulfilled the same hour on Nebuchadnezzar. He was driven from men and ate grass like oxen; and his body was wet with the dew of the sky until his hair had grown like eagles’ feathers, and his nails like birds’ claws.

hold.question: Should WEB Dan.4.28 remain the opening of Dan.4.28-Dan.4.33, or attach backward to create Dan.4.19-Dan.4.28 followed by Dan.4.29-Dan.4.33?
options: Keep Dan.4.28-Dan.4.33 so the fulfillment formula introduces the narrated realization and never stands alone.
Use Dan.4.19-Dan.4.28 plus Dan.4.29-Dan.4.33 so the pe-closed formula completes the interpretation before the twelve-month scene.

primary_reviews.support: The fulfillment formula is compact, pe-closed, and immediately followed by the twelve-month realization.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its backward anaphora and forward announcement support opposite attachments without an independent local witness.

challenges.claim: The active forward ownership may overread a marker that also closes the preceding interpretation.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Submit the two non-overlapping routes to external Aramaic and human review.

primary_reviews.support: Fulfillment summary, delay, boast, interruption, and completed abasement make a coherent realization movement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The formula at 4:28 can also function as an epilogue to Daniel's interpretation.

primary_reviews.support: Either option remains safe if the complete proclamation parent and restoration sibling are mandatory.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: An incorrect exclusive attachment could conceal the hinge's bidirectional discourse function.

challenges.claim: Retrieval metadata may falsely present one versification treatment as settled.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Preserve the appeal and annotate backward as well as forward hydration until adjudicated.

deciding_marker_or_seam: At the end of the stated period, first-person testimony resumes with lifted eyes, restored understanding, renewed rule, and praise that closes the royal proclamation at 4:37.
boundary_rationale: The restored voice begins a distinct closing testimony at 4:34 and carries through the final praise, so I separate it from narrated abasement without severing either from the complete dream proclamation.
rejected_alternative: Keeping 4:28-37 as one child would hide the abasement-to-restoration reversal at 4:34, while isolating only the final praise would detach it from restored reason and kingdom.
defensible_basis: Temporal completion, restored cognition, return of honor and advisers, and renewed praise form the proclamation's reversal and first-person conclusion. The next chapter opens an unrelated feast scene.

source_observations.text: At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me; and I blessed the Most High, and I praised and honored him who lives forever, for his dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom from generation to generation.
Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven; for all his works are truth, and his ways justice; and those who walk in pride he is able to abase.

primary_reviews.support: The time-completion expression and first-person resumption clearly distinguish restoration from the preceding abasement report.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: No MT section marker occurs at the 4:33-34 seam, and the reversal completes the same fulfillment arc.

primary_reviews.support: Understanding, praise, restored status, and final confession produce one restorative testimony.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its meaning depends on dream, interpretation, realization, and loss narrated earlier.

primary_reviews.support: The selected child keeps restored rule and doxology together rather than offering praise alone.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A user may still retrieve the last verse without the proclamation's pride and abasement context.

challenges.claim: The final praise is vulnerable to decontextualized quotation.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Attach the complete Daniel 4 proclamation whenever 4:37 is surfaced.

deciding_marker_or_seam: The feast uses the Jerusalem vessels, praise is directed to manufactured gods, a hand writes on the wall, and summoned wise men fail, leaving the king terrified at 5:9.
boundary_rationale: I hold the feast and failed first response together because the writing crisis is not complete until the court experts cannot read it; the queen's entrance at 5:10 supplies the next speaker and remedy.
rejected_alternative: A division at the summons in 5:7 would split sign from failed interpretation, whereas continuing to 5:10 would cross into the queen's new advisory speech.
defensible_basis: Banquet, vessel command, collective praise, sudden sign, bodily fear, promised reward, and interpretive failure constitute one disruption scene. The unresolved crisis prompts a new entrant next.

source_observations.text: Belshazzar the king made a great feast to a thousand of his lords, and drank wine before the thousand.
Then King Belshazzar was greatly troubled, and his face was changed in him, and his lords were perplexed.

primary_reviews.support: The sign, reward formula, wise-men failure, and royal agitation remain one unresolved Aramaic court crisis.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A samekh after 5:7 marks the summons internally but does not resolve the writing.

primary_reviews.support: Feast conduct, supernatural disruption, and inability to interpret create a single scene awaiting a competent reader.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The vessel use and praise list have thematic weight that can tempt premature subdivision.

primary_reviews.support: Temple vessels and writing remain embedded in the narrated feast before any relation to Kings, Chronicles, or Jeremiah.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: No kinship, imperial chronology, historical harmonization, or fulfillment claim follows from the boundary.

deciding_marker_or_seam: The queen enters because of the court's alarm, recommends Daniel with a retrospective characterization, and the king summons him, restates the failure, and offers reward through 5:16.
boundary_rationale: The queen's counsel and king's commission remain one bridge from failed court wisdom to Daniel's answer, ending before he rejects the offered gifts and reframes the sign at 5:17.
rejected_alternative: Splitting after the queen's speech at 5:12 would separate recommendation from its enacted summons, while extending to 5:17 would absorb Daniel's refusal and indictment into the invitation.
defensible_basis: Advisor entry, identification of a qualified interpreter, direct royal address, problem restatement, and incentive form a complete summons exchange. Daniel becomes the active speaker only afterward.

source_observations.text: The queen by reason of the words of the king and his lords came into the banquet house. The queen spoke and said, “O king, live forever; don’t let your thoughts trouble you, nor let your face be changed.

But I have heard of you, that you can give interpretations and dissolve doubts. Now if you can read the writing and make known to me its interpretation, you shall be clothed with purple, and have a chain of gold around your neck, and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom.”

primary_reviews.support: Queen speech, formal summons, and renewed offer of status lead continuously to Daniel's response.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The pe after 5:12 and speaker change at 5:13 preserve two internal speech phases.

primary_reviews.support: Recommendation and royal commissioning jointly recruit the interpreter who answers in the following unit.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The queen's remembered characterization could be indexed internally but is not a complete scene alone.

primary_reviews.support: A complete summons guards the remembered court history from being presented as an independent identity claim.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Titles and recollections are character speech and do not authorize historical or theological conclusions.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Daniel refuses the gifts, recounts a prior royal warning, indicts the present king, reads the inscription, and completes its three-part interpretation at 5:28.
boundary_rationale: I end Daniel's response with the final interpreted word because the indictment and inscription explanation are one commissioned answer, while the promised honor and regime reversal begin a narrated consequence.
rejected_alternative: Continuing through 5:31 would mix interpretation with investiture, death, and accession; cutting at 5:23 or 5:24 would sever accusation from the sign whose meaning completes it.
defensible_basis: Refusal, retrospective comparison, ethical charge, presentation of the written words, and their explanation form a single forensic speech. Royal action in 5:29 answers rather than continues that speech.

source_observations.text: Then Daniel answered before the king, “Let your gifts be to yourself, and give your rewards to another. Nevertheless, I will read the writing to the king, and make known to him the interpretation.
PERES: your kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians.”

primary_reviews.support: The answer formula carries refusal, charge, inscription, and interpretation through the final explanation at 5:28.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Wordplay and qere-ketiv pressure in the chapter cannot determine a preferred reading without absent versional evidence.

primary_reviews.support: Daniel's full speech supplies both moral frame and semantic interpretation before the court enacts its response.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The outcome verifies the speech and must remain accessible through the feast-tale parent.

primary_reviews.support: The complete indictment prevents the famous written words from surfacing without their local narrative explanation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: No ruler identity, date, empire equation, or canonical fulfillment is licensed by this segmentation.

deciding_marker_or_seam: The old court grants honor, its king dies, Darius receives the kingdom, appoints administrators, and finds Daniel distinguished through 6:3; officials begin seeking a charge at 6:4.
boundary_rationale: I select the larger 5:29-6:3 transition because it spans old-court honor, death, accession, and new-court elevation, but hold that choice since correlated WLC-family evidence cannot adjudicate its rival versification treatments.
rejected_alternative: The received-coordinate route 5:29-31 plus 6:1-9 and the MT-aligned 5:29-30 plus 5:31-6:9 remain viable; a free-standing 5:31 bridge is rejected as too thin.
defensible_basis: A non-overlapping cross-chapter child lets WEB 5:31 or MT 6:1 perform both backward regime-fall and forward accession work without assigning it exclusively to either tale. Appointment and Daniel's elevation complete the transition before conspiracy starts.

source_observations.text: Then Belshazzar commanded, and they clothed Daniel with purple, and put a chain of gold about his neck, and made proclamation concerning him, that he should be the third ruler in the kingdom.
Then this Daniel was distinguished above the presidents and the local governors, because an excellent spirit was in him; and the king thought to set him over the whole realm.

hold.question: Should the active Dan.5.29-Dan.6.3 transition remain, or should exact coverage use Dan.5.29-Dan.5.31 followed by Dan.6.1-Dan.6.9 with mandatory bridge hydration?
options: Retain Dan.5.29-Dan.6.3 and Dan.6.4-Dan.6.9 so honor, death, accession, appointment, and elevation form one cross-chapter transition before conspiracy.
Use the received-coordinate children Dan.5.29-Dan.5.31 and Dan.6.1-Dan.6.9 while hydrating WEB 5:31 or MT 6:1 bidirectionally into both court tales.

primary_reviews.support: WEB 5:31 corresponds to MT 6:1 and functions as a regnal-receipt bridge before appointments.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: OSHB and UXLC share a textual family and cannot independently choose forward, backward, or bridging ownership.

challenges.claim: The cross-chapter span may privilege a synthetic transition over both received chapter arrangements.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Keep both non-overlapping alternatives in the external and human review docket.

primary_reviews.support: Investiture, same-night death, accession, appointment, and Daniel's elevation trace a coherent status-and-regime transition.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The honor and death also close the feast tale, while appointments launch the new conspiracy plot.

primary_reviews.support: The chosen bridge avoids leaving the accession verse naked and can hydrate to both complete court tales.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Cross-chapter resegmentation could look like a historical or ruler-identity ruling rather than retrieval design.

challenges.claim: Neither WEB nor MT numbering may be presented as literary authority.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Label the active bridge candidate-only and preserve the received split plus the 5:31-6:9 proposal as dissents.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Officials begin seeking an administrative fault at 6:4, conclude that only Daniel's law observance offers leverage, assemble before the king, and secure the signed prohibition at 6:9.
boundary_rationale: I begin with the active search for an accusation and close with the king's signature because those actions build and legally fix the trap; the preceding appointments remain available through the chapter parent.
rejected_alternative: Beginning at 6:1 would repeat accession and appointment material assigned to the held transition, while ending at 6:5 would separate the conspirators' diagnosis from the petition they design.
defensible_basis: The failed search, chosen vulnerability, collective approach, deceptive representation, proposed penalty, and irrevocable signature form one trap-construction scene. Daniel's response starts afterward.

source_observations.text: Then the presidents and the local governors sought to find occasion against Daniel as touching the kingdom; but they could find no occasion or fault, because he was faithful. There wasn’t any error or fault found in him.
Therefore King Darius signed the writing and the decree.

primary_reviews.support: The search-for-ground formula at 6:4 begins a new action after elevation, and the signed writing closes the petition sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A samekh after WEB 6:5 marks an internal turn from failed investigation to petition strategy.

primary_reviews.support: Jealous investigation, selected vulnerability, manipulative petition, and enacted decree make one conspiracy scene.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The trap depends on the appointment context and points directly to Daniel's customary prayer.

primary_reviews.support: The segment keeps the legal prohibition with its conspiratorial manufacture rather than presenting it as neutral law.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Historical administration and legal custom are not inferred from literary form.

deciding_marker_or_seam: After learning the writing is signed, Daniel prays as before; conspirators observe, accuse, and invoke the decree, while the distressed king works until sunset but cannot rescue him.
boundary_rationale: The prayer belongs with the surveillance and court response it precipitates, closing when the king's efforts fail; the command to bring Daniel at 6:16 opens the den ordeal rather than extending deliberation.
rejected_alternative: Separating prayer at 6:10 from surveillance and accusation would remove its legal trigger and consequences, whereas continuing into 6:16 would cross from failed resistance to sentence execution.
defensible_basis: Known decree, customary practice, planned observation, formal charge, royal recognition of the trap, and unsuccessful effort to deliver Daniel form a complete action-and-accusation movement.

source_observations.text: When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.
Then these men assembled together to the king, and said to the king, “Know, O king, that it is a law of the Medes and Persians, that no decree nor statute which the king establishes may be changed.”

primary_reviews.support: The after-he-knew temporal frame joins prayer to the signed decree and the accusers' observation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A samekh after WEB 6:10 can mark prayer before surveillance, but the latter depends on the former.

primary_reviews.support: Counter-action, discovery, accusation, and failed royal maneuvering trace one trap-springing scene.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The den outcome is needed to complete the peril generated here.

primary_reviews.support: Keeping prayer with decree awareness and accusation protects its narrative function.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 6:10 is frequently retrieved as a devotional rule apart from conspiracy and consequence.

challenges.claim: Customary prayer could be universalized as a fixed prescription.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Require 6:10-15 and the full Daniel 6 tale whenever the prayer verse surfaces.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Daniel is cast into and sealed within the den, the king fasts and returns at dawn, Daniel answers, is lifted out unharmed, and the accusers' household reversal concludes at 6:24.
boundary_rationale: I keep the den episode through the disturbing counter-judgment so deliverance is not sanitized from its narrated violence, then place the distinct proclamation and tenure notice in the following coda.
rejected_alternative: Retaining 6:16-28 whole would merge ordeal and violent reversal with the new royal letter at 6:25; ending at release in 6:23 would omit the story's immediate counter-judgment.
defensible_basis: Sentence, seal, vigil, anxious inquiry, testimony, release, inspection, and punishment of the accusers form the full peril-to-reversal action sequence. A universal address begins only afterward.

source_observations.text: Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel and cast him into the den of lions. The king spoke and said to Daniel, “Your God whom you serve continually, he will deliver you.”

The king commanded, and they brought those men who had accused Daniel, and they cast them into the den of lions—them, their children, and their wives; and the lions mauled them, and broke all their bones in pieces before they came to the bottom of the den.

primary_reviews.support: Casting, sealing, dawn inquiry, answer, removal, and counter-sentence remain one continuous action sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The release at 6:23 is an internal resolution before the violent reversal in 6:24.

primary_reviews.support: The ordeal and immediate reversal complete before the proclamation form begins at 6:25.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Counter-judgment and letter are both consequences of deliverance and could remain in one larger close.

challenges.claim: Separating the royal letter may weaken the tale's full public reversal.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Keep 6:16-24 and 6:25-28 linked under Daniel 6.

primary_reviews.support: The selected end refuses to detach rescue from the accusers' violent fate.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: No miracle mechanics, ethical vindication, or universal persecution template is inferred.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Darius addresses all peoples at 6:25, issues a decree with hymnic rationale, recalls the den rescue, and the narrator closes with Daniel's prosperity under two reign labels.
boundary_rationale: I expose the royal letter as a complete aftermath so decree, praise, rescue reference, and tenure remain together; mandatory chapter hydration prevents its claims from floating free of conspiracy and violence.
rejected_alternative: Absorbing 6:25-28 into the den ordeal would hide the change to public-letter form, while isolating the praise clauses would remove decree, rescue reference, and tenure close.
defensible_basis: Universal address, policy command, doxological grounds, backward reference to deliverance, and final prosperity constitute one proclamation coda. The next chapter resets to a dated first-person vision.

source_observations.text: Then King Darius wrote to all the peoples, nations, and languages who dwell in all the earth: “Peace be multiplied to you.
So this Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian.

primary_reviews.support: The address formula inaugurates a unified decree-and-praise register that reaches the prosperity colophon.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its content presupposes the den action and cannot stand as independent royal theology.

primary_reviews.support: A universal letter and tenure notice are formally distinguishable from the preceding ordeal.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: They complete the same tale's political and public consequences.

challenges.claim: The coda could be misread as detached praise material.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Attach conspiracy, prayer, den, rescue, and reversal through the full parent.

primary_reviews.support: The boundary keeps fear-command, divine praise, rescue claim, and prosperity in one ethically textured closure.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Chronological reconciliation of the reign labels remains outside this review.

deciding_marker_or_seam: A dated first-person dream report opens with four winds, sea, and four beasts, then follows the fourth beast to its horns and the speaking little horn through 7:8.
boundary_rationale: I preserve the entire beast sequence because its symbols accumulate toward the horn without self-contained subreports; the throne vision at 7:9 supplies a stronger scene transition than any animal boundary.
rejected_alternative: Individual beasts or horns should not become retrieval atoms; extending through 7:9 would cross from the terrestrial symbolic sequence into the newly set heavenly court scene.
defensible_basis: Date, dream framing, cumulative beast appearances, focused fourth-beast observation, and final horn development form the first visionary panel. Throne placement changes location, imagery, and action next.

source_observations.text: In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon, Daniel had a dream and visions of his head while on his bed. Then he wrote the dream and told the sum of the matters.

“I considered the horns, and behold, there came up among them another horn, a little one, before which three of the first horns were plucked up by the roots; and behold, in this horn were eyes like the eyes of a man, and a mouth speaking arrogantly.

primary_reviews.support: First-person seeing formulas and the cumulative animal register continue through the horn's eyes and speech.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Each beast is internally described and may support navigation without becoming a separate top-level object.

primary_reviews.support: The sequence moves from sea disturbance through four beasts to the focal horn before the visionary camera changes.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The next heavenly scene judges material introduced here, so the full vision parent is essential.

primary_reviews.support: One symbolic panel reduces the risk of assigning identities from isolated beast or horn details.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Canonical echoes to Psalms, Ezekiel, the Gospels, or Revelation remain evidence-only possibilities.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Thrones are placed, the court sits, books open, the beast is judged, and a human-like figure approaches with clouds and receives enduring dominion through 7:14.
boundary_rationale: The court vision remains intact because judgment and dominion are coordinated actions in one scene, and the frequently cited 7:13-14 panel requires the thrones and books that frame its function.
rejected_alternative: Splitting at 7:11 or isolating 7:13-14 would detach dominion from court, books, and beast judgment; beginning earlier would merge sea-beast imagery with the throne scene.
defensible_basis: A coherent heavenly setting joins enthronement, judicial action, beast outcome, cloud-borne approach, presentation, and dominion grant. Daniel's distress at 7:15 shifts from seeing to seeking explanation.

source_observations.text: “I watched until thrones were placed, and one who was Ancient of Days sat. His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool. His throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire.

Dominion was given him, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which will not pass away, and his kingdom one that will not be destroyed.

primary_reviews.support: Vision verbs, court actions, and the dominion grant maintain a single Aramaic scene through 7:14.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The beast's destruction at 7:11-12 looks backward and keeps this panel linked to 7:1-8.

primary_reviews.support: Thrones, judgment, approach, presentation, and grant provide a complete heavenly-court movement.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The interpretation later revisits each symbol and controls the scene's place in the whole vision.

primary_reviews.support: The span preserves the immediate visionary frame for the cloud approach and dominion language.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Later canonical reuse makes 7:13-14 especially vulnerable to naked retrieval and identity overclaim.

challenges.claim: A famous two-verse panel may bypass the court and interpretation.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Hydrate 7:9-14 plus the complete 7:1-28 vision before presenting canonical relations.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Daniel is distressed, approaches an attendant, asks for certainty, and receives a concise four-beast and holy-ones interpretation ending at 7:18; a second focused inquiry starts at 7:19.
boundary_rationale: I expose the first interpretive round because it reaches a compact answer before Daniel asks again about particular symbols; mandatory vision-parent hydration prevents the concise summary from replacing the fuller explanation.
rejected_alternative: Retaining 7:15-28 would obscure the explicit renewed desire to know at 7:19, yet treating the first answer independently would detach it from the second and the vision it explains.
defensible_basis: Emotional reaction, approach, request, short global interpretation, and its completion form one question-answer exchange. The next verse restarts with focused interest in the fourth beast and horn.

source_observations.text: “As for me, Daniel, my spirit was grieved within my body, and the visions of my head troubled me.
But the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom, and possess the kingdom forever, even forever and ever.’

primary_reviews.support: The renewed inquiry formula at 7:19 clearly distinguishes a second interpretive round.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: No MT section marker follows 7:18, and both exchanges explain the same dream.

challenges.claim: The short first answer could be mistaken for a sufficient interpretation of the whole vision.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Require the 7:19-28 sibling and 7:1-28 parent in every retrieval.

primary_reviews.support: Distress, approach, request, and concise answer constitute a finished first dialogue round.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Its generality prompts rather than eliminates the focused second question.

primary_reviews.support: A hydrated child makes the summary navigable without letting it govern identities or fulfillment claims.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Holy-ones and kingdom language remain interpretation-sensitive and cannot stand alone.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Daniel requests certainty about the fourth beast, horns, and speaking horn; the attendant answers through kingdom, conflict, judgment, and dominion, followed by the end-of-matter distress colophon at 7:28.
boundary_rationale: The second inquiry stays whole through Daniel's closing reaction because the detailed interpretation answers the focused question and the colophon expressly terminates the matter rather than opening another scene.
rejected_alternative: Merging backward into 7:15-18 would flatten two dialogue rounds, while splitting the horn, time expression, judgment, or closing reaction would encourage identity and chronology atomization.
defensible_basis: Focused question, recalled observations, extended answer, court outcome, and explicit end formula complete the second exchange and entire vision report. The next chapter resets date, place, and symbols.

source_observations.text: “Then I desired to know the truth concerning the fourth animal, which was different from all of them, exceedingly terrible, whose teeth were of iron, and its nails of bronze; which devoured, broke in pieces, and stamped the residue with its feet;
“Here is the end of the matter. As for me, Daniel, my thoughts troubled me greatly, and my face was changed in me; but I kept the matter in my heart.”

primary_reviews.support: The renewed Aramaic inquiry at 7:19 and end-of-matter formula at 7:28 bracket a full exchange.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Qere-ketiv pressure and no intervening section mark require caution about internal symbol clauses.

challenges.claim: The split from 7:15-18 lacks a formal section break.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Treat it as a dialogue-round seam and preserve the complete vision parent, not as source stratification.

primary_reviews.support: Specific inquiry, detailed symbolic explanation, judicial close, and reaction make a coherent final interpretation round.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Every explained symbol refers back to the earlier vision panels.

primary_reviews.support: Keeping horn, conflict, time formula, judgment, and dominion together limits proof-text extraction.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: No beast, horn, saint, kingdom, or schedule is identified by this boundary.

deciding_marker_or_seam: A new dated vision locates Daniel at Susa, narrates ram, goat, broken horn and successors, follows the growing horn's sanctuary action, and ends with the overheard duration answer at 8:14.
boundary_rationale: I retain the full symbolic report through the internal question because its duration answer depends on the sanctuary action just narrated, while Daniel's interpretive encounter has a fresh onset at 8:15.
rejected_alternative: Splitting individual animals, horns, or the 8:13-14 question would atomize a cumulative symbol report; continuing to 8:15 would cross from vision content into Daniel's search for understanding and messenger commission.
defensible_basis: Superscription, location, symbolic conflict, horn development, cultic action, and intravision dialogue comprise what Daniel sees before interpretation begins. The desire to understand changes the scene's function next.

source_observations.text: In the third year of the reign of King Belshazzar, a vision appeared to me, even to me, Daniel, after that which appeared to me at the first.
He said to me, “To two thousand and three hundred evenings and mornings. Then the sanctuary will be cleansed.”

primary_reviews.support: Hebrew vision framing and symbol sequence continue into the overheard holy-one exchange through 8:14.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The question at 8:13 is a real internal speech shift and may support navigation.

primary_reviews.support: The complete ram-goat-horn report reaches its own question and answer before messenger interpretation begins.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The symbols remain unexplained until the following encounter, so the chapter parent is mandatory.

primary_reviews.support: The broad span resists isolating sanctuary action or the duration formula from the vision sequence.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Number and offering queries may still bypass the complete report and interpretation.

challenges.claim: The 8:13-14 answer can be converted into a calculation atom.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Hydrate both 8:1-14 and 8:15-27 without selecting chronology or fulfillment.

deciding_marker_or_seam: Daniel seeks understanding, Gabriel is commissioned, touch and speech restore him, symbols are interpreted, sealing is commanded, and the resulting sickness, recovery, court work, and incomprehension close at 8:27.
boundary_rationale: I merge the one-verse aftermath into the interpretation because illness, return to duty, wonder, and lack of understanding all presuppose the messenger's disclosure and cannot carry retrieval context independently.
rejected_alternative: The baseline's standalone 8:27 coda is rejected as referentially dependent; ending at 8:26 would sever the vision encounter from its narrated bodily and vocational aftermath.
defensible_basis: Commission, repeated strengthening, explanation, sealing, and first-person effect form a complete interpretation event. The pe only after 8:27 and the new dated scene at 9:1 corroborate the larger close.

source_observations.text: When I, even I Daniel, had seen the vision, I sought to understand it. Then behold, there stood before me someone with the appearance of a man.
I, Daniel, fainted, and was sick for some days. Then I rose up and did the king’s business. I wondered at the vision, but no one understood it.

primary_reviews.support: No section mark closes at 8:26; first-person effects continue until the pe after 8:27.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Direct messenger speech ends with the sealing command, so the final verse remains a distinct internal coda.

primary_reviews.support: The aftermath records the interpretation encounter's effect and closes the report rather than beginning a new episode.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: A shift from speech to later life does provide an annotatable form change.

primary_reviews.support: The merge eliminates a one-verse fragment whose sickness and wonder would otherwise lack their referent.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: No medical, psychological, ruler, event, or fulfillment inference follows from the coda.

deciding_marker_or_seam: A regnal date leads to Daniel's understanding of Jeremiah's seventy years, then he turns his face toward God with prayer, fasting, sackcloth, and ashes through 9:3.
boundary_rationale: I retain reading and orientation together because Jeremiah's word prompts the prayer posture, while the actual confessional speech begins at 9:4 and should not erase its narrated occasion.
rejected_alternative: Joining the frame directly to 9:4-19 would hide the explicit scriptural and ascetic preparation; isolating 9:1-2 would separate reading from the prayer posture it produces.
defensible_basis: Date, book reading, identified prophetic word, numerical observation, and embodied turn toward petition form the prayer's initiating frame. The quoted confession begins with a new direct address at 9:4.

source_observations.text: In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, of the offspring of the Medes, who was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans—
I set my face to the Lord God, to seek by prayer and petitions, with fasting and sackcloth and ashes.

primary_reviews.support: The return to Hebrew after chapter 7 is already established; here date, books, and prayer orientation remain one prose frame.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The seventy-year wording carries translation and canonical pressure that cannot decide chronology.

primary_reviews.support: Reading produces understanding, which produces the embodied turn toward prayer before direct speech starts.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The frame has no complete response without the confession and messenger answer that follow.

primary_reviews.support: The span keeps the explicit Jeremiah reading joined to prayer orientation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Numerical and regnal details invite date calculation or historical harmonization.

challenges.claim: The seventy-year reference could become an isolated chronology input.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Attach the whole Daniel 9 prayer-response parent and Jeremiah context without selecting a schedule.

deciding_marker_or_seam: The prayer opens by addressing God, moves through corporate confession and acknowledged judgment, recalls exodus and covenant mercy, and culminates in repeated pleas to hear, forgive, and act at 9:19.
boundary_rationale: The confession remains whole because accusation, acknowledgment, remembered mercy, and petition build one prayer rather than detachable doctrinal sections; the narration resumes only after its urgent close.
rejected_alternative: Dividing confession, rationale, and petition would fragment one uninterrupted prayer; extending through 9:20 would cross from quoted address into narration of the prayer's ongoing delivery.
defensible_basis: First-person plural confession, contrast between divine righteousness and communal shame, scriptural curse language, historical appeal, and escalating petitions form a sustained rhetorical whole with a clear final imperative cluster.

source_observations.text: I prayed to Yahweh my God, and made confession, and said, “Oh, Lord, the great and dreadful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with those who love him and keep his commandments,
Lord, hear. Lord, forgive. Lord, listen and do. Don’t defer, for your own sake, my God, because your city and your people are called by your name.”

primary_reviews.support: Repeated first-person plural forms and direct address sustain one Hebrew prayer through the final plea.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Internal shifts from confession to appeal to petition are rhetorically real but remain subordinate movements.

primary_reviews.support: Corporate confession, explanation of judgment, remembered deliverance, and urgent petitions form a continuous liturgical address.

deciding_marker_or_seam: While Daniel is still praying, Gabriel arrives, explains his commission to give understanding, and delivers the seventy-weeks discourse through its decreed-end conclusion at 9:27.
boundary_rationale: I keep encounter and oracle together because the numbered disclosure is explicitly commissioned as a response while Daniel prays; its difficult clauses remain within the full answer rather than becoming calculation fragments.
rejected_alternative: Beginning a child at 9:24 would detach the numbers from messenger arrival and commission; splitting individual weeks, decrees, figures, covenant, or abomination clauses would encode disputed readings as boundaries.
defensible_basis: Prayer-time narration, touch, instruction, beloved-address, command to understand, and the complete compressed oracle constitute one answer event. A new dated revelation begins only in chapter 10.

source_observations.text: While I was speaking, praying, and confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and presenting my supplication before Yahweh my God for the holy mountain of my God—

He will make a firm covenant with many for one week. In the middle of the week he will cause the sacrifice and the offering to cease. On the wing of abominations will come one who makes desolate; and even to the decreed full end, wrath will be poured out on the desolate.”

primary_reviews.support: The while-I-was-speaking frame and messenger commission directly introduce the numbered Hebrew discourse.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Punctuation, lexical, and textual questions in 9:24-27 remain unresolved without independent versional apparatus.

primary_reviews.support: Arrival, authorization, command to understand, and complete oracle operate as one commissioned reply to prayer.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Verse 9:24 begins a distinct numbered speech movement suitable for internal navigation.

deciding_marker_or_seam: The superscription dates and summarizes a true message of great conflict, then Daniel narrates three completed weeks of mourning, restricted food, and no anointing; a pe follows 10:3.
boundary_rationale: I expose the superscription-mourning frame because its period closes before the apparition receives a new date and place; the larger 10-12 revelation prevents preparation from becoming a detached ascetic rule.
rejected_alternative: Retaining 10:1-9 would cross the marked completion of mourning into a separately dated river encounter at 10:4, though both remain joined by the final-revelation parent.
defensible_basis: Third-person message summary and first-person mourning specify occasion and preparation before the exact day and river location change. The completed three-week period gives the frame a formal terminus.

source_observations.text: In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia a message was revealed to Daniel, whose name was called Belteshazzar; and the message was true, even a great warfare. He understood the message, and had understanding of the vision.
I ate no pleasant food. No meat or wine came into my mouth. I didn’t anoint myself at all, until three whole weeks were fulfilled.

primary_reviews.support: A pe after 10:3 and the fresh day-and-place formula at 10:4 corroborate the seam.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The mourning duration is recalled by the messenger and prepares the encounter.

challenges.claim: The short frame could be detached from the disclosure it introduces.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Require Dan.10.1-12.13 and the 10:4-9 sibling during retrieval.

primary_reviews.support: Dated summary, three-week mourning, and completed abstentions create a full preparation movement.

deciding_marker_or_seam: A new exact day and river location introduce the linen-clothed figure, Daniel alone sees while companions flee, strength leaves him, and hearing the voice brings a face-down sleep at 10:9.
boundary_rationale: The river apparition closes with Daniel incapacitated before contact, so I distinguish it from the repeated touch-and-speech restoration that follows while retaining the entire final revelation as context.
rejected_alternative: Merging backward would suppress the date-location reset; extending to 10:10 would cross from apparition and collapse into a new hand-touch and restoration dialogue.
defensible_basis: Setting, visual description, differential perception, flight, bodily depletion, heard voice, and collapse form an encounter panel. A hand intervenes next, changing action from overwhelming appearance to strengthening speech.

source_observations.text: In the twenty-fourth day of the first month, as I was by the side of the great river, which is Hiddekel,
Yet I heard the voice of his words. When I heard the voice of his words, then I fell into a deep sleep on my face, with my face toward the ground.

primary_reviews.support: The exact date and river formula open a scene after the pe, and the hand at 10:10 initiates another phase.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: No section marker closes at 10:9, and the same encounter continues.

challenges.claim: The seam may overstate a phase boundary inside one uninterrupted apparition.
challenges.proposed_remedy: Keep both encounter children under the complete 10:1-12:13 parent.
